content: During menopause, the declining response of ovarian follicles typically results in fluctuating and eventually reduced estrogen levels. This hormonal change can lead to various symptoms, such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) is a precursor to androgens, which are subsequently converted into testosterone and estrogens. Administering DHEA has been hypothesized to increase estrogen and testosterone levels in periand postmenopausal women, potentially alleviating their symptoms and enhancing overall well-being and sexual function, including libido, dyspareunia, and satisfaction. However, the use of DHEA as a treatment remains controversial due to uncertainties regarding its efficacy and safety. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of DHEA in managing menopausal symptoms in periand postmenopausal women. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, and LILACS, as well as conference abstracts and trial registries. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing any dose and form of DHEA to placebo, no treatment, or other active interventions were included, provided the treatment duration was at least seven days. A total of 28 trials involving 1,273 menopausal women were included in the review, with data from 16 trials used for meta-analysis. The overall quality of the studies ranged from moderate to low. When compared to placebo, DHEA did not significantly improve quality of life (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.16, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.03 to 0.34, P = 0.10). The evidence for this outcome was of moderate quality, and one trial judged to have a high risk of bias was excluded in a sensitivity analysis. DHEA was associated with androgenic side effects, primarily acne, when compared to placebo (odds ratio [OR] 3.77, 95% CI 1.36 to 10.4, P = 0.01). However, no associations were found with other adverse effects. The impact of DHEA on menopausal symptoms was unclear due to inconsistent results across trials and differences in measurement methods (e.g., continuous, dichotomous, change, and end scores). DHEA was found to improve sexual function compared to placebo (SMD 0.31, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.55, P = 0.01). This finding was based on five studies involving 261 women, and one trial with a high risk of bias was excluded during sensitivity analysis. When comparing oral DHEA to skin-applied DHEA, no significant differences in acne occurrence were observed (OR 2.16, 95% CI 0.47 to 9.96, P = 0.90 for oral DHEA; OR 2.74, 95% CI 0.10 to 74.87, P = 0.90 for skin-applied DHEA). The evidence for these comparisons was of very low quality. Similarly, no significant differences in sexual function were observed when comparing oral DHEA (SMD 0.11, 95% CI -0.13 to 0.35, P = 0.36) to intravaginal DHEA (SMD 0.42, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.81). Insufficient data were available to assess quality of life and menopausal symptoms for these comparisons. There was also insufficient evidence to compare the effects of DHEA to hormone therapy (HT) on quality of life, menopausal symptoms, and adverse effects. No substantial differences in sexual function were observed when comparing DHEA to HT (mean difference [MD] 1.26, 95% CI -0.21 to 2.73, P = 0.09). In conclusion, there is no evidence to suggest that DHEA improves quality of life in perior postmenopausal women. While DHEA may slightly improve sexual function compared to placebo, it is associated with androgenic side effects, such as acne. The evidence regarding its impact on menopausal symptoms remains inconclusive due to inconsistencies in the available data.
